'''Minerva Cordero Braña''' <ref>{{Cite web|title=Minerva Cordero-Epperson – Academy of Distinguished Teachers – The University of Texas at Arlington|url=http://www.uta.edu/academy/members/2005/minerva-cordero-epperson.php|access-date=2020-07-12|website=www.uta.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Links|url=https://wweb.uta.edu/faculty/cordero/links.htm|access-date=2020-07-12|website=wweb.uta.edu}}</ref> is a Puerto Rican mathematician and a professor of mathematics at the [[University of Texas at Arlington]]. She is also the university's Senior Associate Dean for the College of Science, where she is responsible for the advancement of the research mission of the college.<ref name="UTA">{{Cite web|url=http://www.uta.edu/cos/news.php?ID=174|title=College of Science|website=www.uta.edu|access-date=2017-04-08}}</ref> President Biden awarded her the [[Presidential Award for Excellence in Science, Mathematics, and Engineering Mentoring]] (PAESMEM) on February 8, 2022.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2022-02-08 |title=President Biden Honors 117 Individuals and Organizations with Highest U.S. Award for Science and Mathematics Teachers and Mentors |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/02/08/president-biden-honors-117-individuals-and-organizations-with-highest-u-s-award-for-science-and-mathematics-teachers-and-mentors/ |access-date=2022-03-31 |website=The White House |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Cordero was born in [[Bayamón, Puerto Rico]]. Her mother, whose schooling stopped after the fifth grade,<ref name=":2" /> made education a top priority in the family home. She told her children "the best thing I can give you is an education."  Cordero and her siblings would do their homework together and discussed what they learned in school each day.<ref name=":2" /> Cordero said, "We learned each other's subjects." Wanting to go to college, Cordero bought herself a college exam preparation book in high school and studied for the college-entrance exam.<ref name=":2" /><ref name="maa" /> She states that her exam scores were the highest scores for her high school, Miguel Melendez Munoz High School.<ref name="maa">{{cite web|last1=Hill|first1=Vicki|title=Minerva-Cordero Epperson|url=http://www.maa.org/minerva-cordero-epperson|website=MAA|publisher=Mathematical Association of America|accessdate=4 May 2017}}</ref>

Cordero attended the Universidad de Puerto Rico in Rio Piedras and received her B.S. in Mathematics in 1981. She was granted a National Science Foundation Minority Graduate Fellowship which she used to attend the [[University of California, Berkeley|University of California at Berkeley]] to obtain her masters in mathematics in 1983. She continued her studies at the [[University of Iowa]], and obtained her Ph.D. in mathematics in 1989 under Norman Johnson.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Mathematics PhDs from the University of Iowa (Year) {{!}} Department of Mathematics {{!}} College of Liberal Arts & Sciences {{!}} The University of Iowa|url=https://math.uiowa.edu/graduate-program/mathematics-phds/phdbyyear|access-date=2020-07-12|website=math.uiowa.edu}}</ref><ref name="maa" />

== Career and research ==
Cordero's research is in the area of finite semifields ([[Non-associative algebra|non-associative algebras]]) and their associated planes (viewed affinely or projectively) in the general area of [[finite geometry]].<ref name="SACNAS">{{Cite web|url=http://bio.sacnas.org/biography/Biography.asp?mem=183&type=2|title=SACNAS Biography Project|website=bio.sacnas.org|access-date=2017-04-09}}</ref>

After earning her Ph.D., Cordero worked as an associate and an assistant professor at [[Texas Tech University]] until 2001, when she joined the faculty at the [[University of Texas at Arlington]].<ref name="UTA" /> Cordero served as the [[Mathematical Association of America]]'s Governor-at-Large for Minority Interests from 2008 to 2011.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sites.google.com/site/awmmath/home/awm-elections-2015/minerva-cordero-university-of-texas-at-arlington|title=Minerva Cordero, University of Texas at Arlington – AWM Association for Women in Mathematics|website=sites.google.com|access-date=2017-04-09}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ams.org/profession/prizebooklet-2012.pdf|title=January 2012 Prizes and Awards|date=January 5, 2012|website=American Mathematical Society|access-date=April 9, 2017}}</ref>

Cordero's most-cited work is ''A survey of finite [[semifield]]s''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cordero|first1=M.|last2=Wene|first2=G.P.|title=A survey of finite semifields|journal=Discrete Mathematics|volume=208-209|issue=28 October 1999|pages=125–137|doi=10.1016/S0012-365X(99)00068-0|year=1999|doi-access=free}}</ref> She was the Principal Investigator for a [[National Science Foundation]] grant of $2.85 million awarded to the [[University of Texas at Arlington]] in 2009 for a project that placed mathematics graduate students in [[Arlington, Texas|Arlington]] public schools to enhance teaching and learning in the classrooms and to inspire students to pursue careers in [[Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics|STEM]] (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics).<ref>{{cite web|last1=Stevens|first1=Sue|title=UT Arlington math department wins $2.85 million NSF grant; project places graduate students in Arlington public schools to improve math teaching|url=http://www.uta.edu/math/gk12/news/nsf_grant_2009.html|website=University of Texas Arlington|accessdate=12 January 2018}}</ref>
